units.text: This book begins at a gaming table and ends up somewhere less comfortable: where we no longer know whether we have obtained a good result or merely a convincing explanation of why the result is supposedly good. It does not claim that using artificial intelligence is inherently gambling. It explores the conditions under which a conversation, a coding session, or a research project takes on the rhythm of “one more try” and asks what remains after the attempts.

The text combines accessible accounts of research with arguments and proposals of its own. Studies are indicated by numbers in square brackets, with active links to the bibliography. An experiment, a survey, a case report, and a simulation are not treated as equivalent evidence. Preliminary papers, called preprints, and situations where the data do not permit a causal conclusion are explicitly marked. Research for this book concluded on September 11, 2026. The selection of literature is narrative, guided by the book’s questions, rather than an exhaustive systematic review.

Dana, Andrei, and Mara, and their experiences, are fictional characters and scenes. They explain possible mechanisms; they are not testimonies collected from users and cannot demonstrate how frequently behaviors occur. Empirical data appear separately. Neither the narrative voice nor AI-assisted writing claims lived human experiences.

The terms “psychosis,” “delusion,” and “mania” have clinical meanings. They are not insults and do not describe simply being wrong, enthusiastic, or proposing an unusual idea. The pages on mental health provide general guidance, not diagnosis or treatment. A significant change in sleep, functioning, or one’s relationship with reality deserves discussion with a professional. The book does not recommend changing any prescribed treatment.

It can be read consecutively, as an essay about our relationship with possibility. It can also be used: Part Five explains how to verify answers, while the appendices offer tools for researchers, programmers, and teams. The idea is not to replace the joy of discovery with forms. It is to prevent the formulation of a discovery from standing in for the discovery itself.
